title: Elementary-time reachability for one-dimensional grammar-controlled VAS
formal: Can reachability for one-dimensional grammar-controlled vector addition systems be decided in elementary deterministic time? More explicitly, do there exist fixed integers \(h\geq0\), \(c\geq1\) and one deterministic Turing machine deciding every instance of bit length \(n\) within \(O(e_h(n^c+c))\) steps, where \(e_0(z)=z\) and \(e_{j+1}(z)=2^{e_j(z)}\)?
why: This asks whether one nonnegative counter interacting with context-free control can still be analyzed within a fixed-height exponential time bound. It separates existence of a decision algorithm from a meaningful complexity boundary and tests whether enormous reachable sets force equally enormous decision time.
status_note: Rechecked on 13 September 2026. General 1-GVAS decidability is established by the later Bizière–Czerwiński paper, superseding the survey’s provisional wording. The selected elementary-time question is explicitly left open there and remains distinguished from the 2026 index-dependent thin-grammar bound. These proof texts were checked for statements and scope, not independently formalized in Lean.

sentences: A context-free grammar specifies integer update sequences for a single nonnegative counter.
Reachability requires a generated sequence that stays nonnegative at every prefix and ends at the exact target value.
General decidability is now established, and this card selects the still-open elementary-time boundary.
The algorithm must have one fixed-height exponential bound for all binary-encoded grammars and endpoints.

definitions: A one-dimensional grammar-controlled vector addition system (1-GVAS) is a finite context-free grammar with nonterminal set \(N\), distinguished start nonterminal \(S\), and finitely many productions \(X\to\alpha\) with \(X\in N\) and \(\alpha\) a finite sequence of nonterminals and integer terminals. There is no restriction on recursion or on the number of nonterminals occurring in a sentential form. The empty right-hand side is allowed. A terminal word \(a_1\cdots a_m\), with \(a_i\in\mathbb Z\), is generated when a finite sequence of production applications transforms \(S\) into that word. Given starting and target counters \(s,t\in\mathbb N\), the word witnesses reachability if \(s+\sum_{i=1}^j a_i\geq0\) for every \(0\leq j\leq m\), and \(s+\sum_{i=1}^m a_i=t\). The terminal order is the left-to-right order in the generated word, not the order in which productions were expanded. An empty terminal word witnesses exactly \(s=t\), if generated. There is one nonnegative counter, no test for zero except through inability to take a negative update, and no restriction on stack depth implicit in the grammar. The whole grammar, both counters and all production sequences are explicit inputs. Integer terminals use signed binary encodings, and \(s,t\) use binary nonnegative encodings; their digits and every symbol occurrence contribute to input length. The tower height \(h\), polynomial exponent \(c\), hidden multiplicative constant and program must be independent of the grammar and both counters. Correctness concerns exact reachability, not coverability or an approximation of the reachable set.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a deterministic decision algorithm with one fixed elementary time bound for all instances, or prove in Lean that no elementary-time decider exists. A bound whose tower height depends on the input grammar or a theorem only for structurally restricted grammars does not establish the positive answer. The output need only decide reachability; it need not print a potentially enormous derivation.

context_blocks.text: The 2024 survey asks broadly for the complexity of 1-GVAS reachability and at that time describes an unconfirmed decidability argument. Editorial specialization: this card selects the elementary-time boundary, explicitly conjectured in the subsequent complete decidability paper. It does not claim that answering this boundary alone determines the exact complexity class.

The counter constrains prefixes, not just the final sum. A generated word \((-1),1\) has total effect zero but is invalid from counter zero. A word \(1,(-1)\) with the same total effect is valid from zero. A grammar’s ordering constraints and counter nonnegativity therefore interact.

Bizière and Czerwiński’s November 2024 paper proves reachability decidable for general 1-GVAS. It constructs a thin grammar with the same reachability relation. A nonterminal is thin if no derivation from it can produce a sentential form containing two copies of that same nonterminal; a grammar is thin when all its nonterminals are thin.

Theorem 2 and Corollary 3 show that an elementary algorithm for thin grammars would imply an elementary algorithm for all 1-GVAS. Thin grammars are already a subclass, so the elementary-time question has the same yes/no answer in the two settings. This is a preservation theorem for the complexity boundary, not an existing elementary bound.

The February 2026 thin-GVAS preprint improves an upper bound parameterized by its structural index and continues to leave an elementary upper bound open. Since that index can grow with the grammar, its stated fast-growing bound does not supply a fixed-height exponential tower for every input.

The survey illustrates small grammars with extremely large finite reachable sets. Such cardinality alone does not prove a matching lower bound for deciding whether one supplied counter value is reachable. Conversely, merely finding short derivations in a collection of examples does not give a uniform decision algorithm.
